sections.h2: Where is the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds office?
sections.html:
The office is in the Dauphin County Courthouse, Room 102, at 101 Market Street in Harrisburg. Staff are there weekdays until half past four, starting at eight, and the number to call is (717) 780-6560.

Everything filed against Dauphin County land passes through this counter or its online equivalent: deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, easements, plans and powers of attorney. The office describes its job narrowly. It records, reproduces and indexes documents that the law allows to be recorded, and it does not give title advice.

A seller who works with a title company will rarely deal with the office directly. The settlement agent prepares the deed, adds the fees and transfer tax, and sends it in.

sections.h2: What does the Dauphin County recorder charge for recording?
sections.html:
Deeds and mortgages each carry an $87.75 fee on the schedule revised December 1, 2025. The schedule says that any document needing a Unified Parcel Identifier adds $20.00 for each identifier, so a one parcel deed totals $107.75.

The office says these fees come from the Commonwealth through the General Assembly and can change over time. A fee calculator on the office web page works out the total for a given document.

sections.h2: How is transfer tax split on a Dauphin County sale?
sections.html:
Per the county FAQ, a 2% levy applies to what is paid for the property. One point belongs to the Department of Revenue, with a half point apiece for the township or borough and the school district.

The state's revenue page adds that both parties to a deed answer for the state's share together, and that the recorder forwards it. The purchase agreement is where a buyer and seller decide who pays.

  • The FAQ lists conveyances between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and brothers and sisters as exempt, and other exemptions exist in special cases.
  • A deed for nominal consideration, such as $1, between tax exempt parties carries $0 of transfer tax and does not need separate checks.
  • State law also exempts property passed by will or by intestate succession, along with burial site deeds and certain transfers to governments.

A $230,000 sale would carry $4,600 at that rate. Have the settlement agent confirm the final figure before closing.

sections.h2: How are fees paid, and when do originals return?
sections.html:
Cash and checks are the accepted ways to pay, and checks name the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds. Anything mailed in needs a stamped return envelope with your address on it, plus the correct amount.

In most cases the original goes back to the person who presented it within a day or two, although busy periods, holidays and staffing can stretch that. If two weeks pass with nothing in hand, the FAQ tells you to ask the firm that filed it.

Large closings often go through a title company, so ask which firm will submit the deed and how it will pay the fees.

sections.h2: How far back do Dauphin County records go?
sections.html:
The first recorded registry dates to 1785. The office website holds deeds and miscellaneous documents from 1785 forward and mortgages from 1979 forward, and it has the deed indexes and a mortgage index online under the Alpha Index.

The FAQ explains the handling of the originals. Each document is scanned and the original is kept until the indexes and records are checked and proofed by at least two people. Images are backed up to hard drive and microfilmed to meet the Pennsylvania Historical Museum Commission requirements, and the microfilm is stored off-site in an underground facility so records can be recreated after a courthouse disaster.

Nearly everything recorded is public. The exception is a military discharge paper, DD214. Search access requires accepting the office's disclaimer, which states that the official records are those held in the office.

sections.h2: What else does the Dauphin County recorder handle besides deeds?
sections.html:
Notaries start here. A new notary brings identification, the completed notary bond and payment, and the office records the bond and commission and administers the oath. The notary then walks to the Prothonotary to register a signature. The FAQ says no appointment is needed, and the filing fee is $33.50 on the schedule.

The office also takes plans at $20.50 for the first page and $5.00 for each page after, and it files Uniform Commercial Code statements at $100.00. Certified copies cost $2.00 plus the per page copy charge, microfilm copies are $0.75 and photocopies are $0.50 a page.

One misunderstanding comes up with burial plots. A cemetery lot deed normally grants permission to use the ground, while the cemetery keeps title, and those papers are held by the cemetery company or association, not by the county.

sections.h2: What common questions come up before a Dauphin County sale?
sections.html:
Several questions repeat at the counter, and the FAQ answers them directly.

  • A change of ownership needs a new deed prepared and recorded. Merely stating a change does nothing.
  • After a mortgage is paid, the lender typically sends a satisfaction to the office. The owner does not get a new deed.
  • If a spouse dies and the couple held title as tenants by the entirety, the survivor generally explains the death in the next deed or mortgage. Other forms of title, such as tenants in common, may need different handling, and the office suggests asking an attorney.
  • A deed for a lot usually covers buildings erected on it, now or later.
  • A deed gives a legal description of boundaries, but a surveyor places markers on the ground.

Anyone can write their own deed, though the office recommends having an attorney prepare it so the recording criteria are met and the right fee is enclosed.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about Dauphin County?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 293,351 people, up from 286,401 in the 2020 count. The county spans 524.87 square miles, which works out to about 545.7 residents per square mile, and it holds 129,660 housing units.

For 2020 to 2024, QuickFacts reports a middle home value of $236,400 among owners, who occupy 63.1% of homes. Renters pay $1,217 in the middle of the range, and the middle household earns $76,242. Permits issued in 2025 numbered 329, and a commute averages 21.5 minutes.

Compared with the neighboring counties on the same table, Dauphin has the lowest median home value and the lowest owner occupancy.

faqs.q: What will a Dauphin County deed cost to record?
faqs.a: The deed fee is $87.75 on the December 1, 2025 revision, with $20.00 added for each Unified Parcel Identifier and $2.00 for every page after the fourth. Transfer tax is figured separately from the sale price.

faqs.q: What transfer tax rate applies in Dauphin County?
faqs.a: The county FAQ gives 2% of the value conveyed, divided as 1% for the state and a half percent each for the municipality and school district. Some transfers between close relatives are exempt.

faqs.q: Does the Recorder of Deeds accept cards?
faqs.a: The county FAQ lists cash and check as accepted payment for recording fees. Make checks payable to Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds. Ask the office by phone before relying on any other method.

faqs.q: When does a recorded deed come back to me?
faqs.a: Within one to two days in most cases, according to the office, though volume, holidays and staffing can add time. After two weeks without your papers, contact whoever submitted them.

faqs.q: Can I search Dauphin County deeds online?
faqs.a: Yes. The office website has deeds and miscellaneous documents from 1785 and mortgages from 1979, searchable after you accept a disclaimer. Military discharge papers are the one category not open to the public.
